stories.headline: Court Blocks National Park Service From Removing Anti-Trump '86 47' Flag Near National Mall
stories.summary:
A federal judge appointed by President Obama issued a temporary restraining order Monday preventing the National Park Service from removing an "86 47" flag flown near the National Mall by progressive activist group Accountability Now USA. U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss found the meaning of "86" ambiguous, noting the flag bore patriotic colors and no violent symbols, and concluded the group was using it to urge Congress to impeach and remove President Trump from office.

The ruling draws the '86 47' symbol into direct legal conflict after the Justice Department charged former FBI Director James Comey over a social media post featuring the same numbers arranged in seashells. The administration has treated "86 47" as a threat against the president, citing the term's use in the restaurant industry to mean removing or refusing service, combined with Trump's status as the 47th president. Comey faces up to ten years in prison if convicted and has denied any violent intent.

The Department of the Interior sharply criticized the ruling. "This opinion is from an Obama-appointed judge. In what world have we lost all decency, to demand that any threat against the President be taken very seriously," a DOI spokesperson told Fox News Digital, while adding that the department would comply with the court's order.

Supporters of the ruling argue it is a straightforward First Amendment protection for political speech, and legal experts have previously warned that the Comey prosecution faces significant constitutional hurdles. Critics contend the symbol constitutes a threat and that allowing its display near the White House perimeter sets a dangerous precedent. The temporary restraining order keeps the flag in place while the broader legal dispute over its meaning continues.

stories.headline: Update: Maine Senate Candidate Graham Platner Hit by Newly Surfaced Drug-Use Admissions in Social Media Posts
stories.summary:
Graham Platner, the presumptive Democratic Senate nominee in Maine, is facing renewed scrutiny after social media posts resurfaced in which he appears to brag about using cocaine and other drugs while traveling through Europe on military leave. In a 2020 Reddit post made under the handle P-Hustle, Platner wrote that he was "backpacking through Europe on the government dime" during terminal leave from the Marine Corps, adding that he "did some drugs and had a blast" and had "no regrets."

A separate 2020 post contains what Fox News characterized as a direct admission to purchasing cocaine. The Marine Corps prohibits servicemen from using or selling illicit drugs, threatening violators with prosecution under the Uniform Code of Military Justice and separation from service. It is unclear whether Platner disclosed the drug use to his superiors. Platner was on the Marine Corps payroll at the time of the trip, according to his own account.

The drug-use disclosures compound a series of controversies that have emerged from Platner's deleted Reddit history, including posts involving infidelity and other content that his campaign has been forced to address. Platner, a combat veteran who also served in the Army National Guard and now farms oysters in Maine, has resisted calls to exit the race. Earlier coverage noted he had met with senators amid separate sexual misconduct allegations.

The episode is shaping up as a test of Democratic Party tolerance for candidate controversy in a competitive Senate race. Platner has the public backing of Sen. Bernie Sanders and has positioned himself as a progressive challenger, but the accumulating controversies have fueled speculation about Maine's ballot replacement rules if he were to withdraw.

stories.headline: George Santos' Prediction-Market Bets on Himself Referred to DOJ for Insider Trading Review
stories.summary:
Betting activity by disgraced former Rep. George Santos on the prediction market platform Kalshi has been referred to the Department of Justice, according to a source familiar with the matter. The referral centers on concerns that Santos may have placed wagers on outcomes related to himself — such as his own legal or political future — using information unavailable to the general public, raising potential insider trading questions.

Santos has become a focal point in a growing national debate about the regulation of political prediction markets. Kalshi and similar platforms allow users to bet real money on political and legal outcomes, and concerns about insider trading by politicians or former officials with privileged access to information have been mounting in Congress and among regulators.

Santos was expelled from the House of Representatives in December 2023 after a House Ethics Committee report found substantial evidence of fraud and other misconduct. He subsequently pleaded guilty to federal charges including wire fraud and identity theft. The new investigation adds a fresh legal dimension to his already extensive post-congressional legal exposure.

The referral reflects wider regulatory anxiety about prediction markets operating with limited oversight in the U.S. Several lawmakers have called for clearer rules governing whether political figures can bet on outcomes they might influence, though no comprehensive federal framework currently exists for this category of financial activity.

stories.headline: CBS News Fires Scott Pelley from 60 Minutes Amid Sweeping Leadership Overhaul
stories.summary:
CBS News fired longtime 60 Minutes anchor Scott Pelley on Tuesday after he publicly accused new management of "murdering" the program at an all-staff meeting the day before. Pelley's termination letter, written by newly installed executive producer Nick Bilton, accused the veteran anchor of "remarkable incivility and contempt" and said he had been uncooperative with the show's new direction.

In a statement following his firing, Pelley alleged that new CBS leadership had pressured him to "inject falsehoods and bias" into his reporting and to include unverified assertions. He described the new management's conduct as marked by "incompetence and unprofessionalism." Bilton, who has no prior broadcast news experience, countered that he had made repeated attempts to find common ground with Pelley and was rebuffed.

The upheaval follows CBS's acquisition by David Ellison — an ally of President Trump — through his purchase of parent company Paramount in August 2025. Ellison subsequently installed media figure Bari Weiss as CBS News chief, who has outlined a vision centered on rebuilding audience trust and shifting away from broadcast-heavy formats. Weiss previously fired 60 Minutes executive producer Tanya Simon and correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega; Vega also alleged management attempted to inject political bias into stories.

The episode has intensified a national debate about media independence and the influence of ownership on editorial decisions. Supporters of the changes argue that legacy broadcast news has lost public trust and requires structural reform; critics contend the firings represent a politically motivated dismantling of one of American journalism's most storied institutions. 60 Minutes is the highest-rated news program in the United States.

stories.headline: Nigeria Court Sentences Four Men to Death for 2022 Catholic Church Massacre
stories.summary:
A federal court in Abuja sentenced four men to death Wednesday for the June 2022 attack on St. Francis Catholic Church in Owo, Ondo State, in which gunmen opened fire and detonated explosives during a Pentecost service, killing 41 worshippers and injuring more than 100 others. The four convicted men — Idris Abdulmalik Omeiza, Al Qasim Idris, Jamiu Abdulmalik, and Abdulhaleem Idris — were also sentenced to 20 years in prison for membership in a terrorist organization.

Judge Emeka Nwite found the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, citing witness testimony including from a survivor who had both legs amputated and lost an eye in the attack. The defendants' lawyers said they would appeal. A fifth defendant was acquitted due to insufficient evidence. During the trial, defendants alleged they had been tortured while in custody, including by electric shock.

The verdict carries symbolic weight beyond Nigeria's borders. The attack was one of the deadliest against Christians in Nigeria in recent years and drew international condemnation. Presidential assent is required before any death sentence is carried out in Nigeria, and no executions have been conducted in the country for several years, raising questions about whether the sentences will be implemented.

The case intersects with ongoing U.S. attention to attacks on Nigerian Christians. President Trump has accused Nigeria of failing to protect its Christian population from jihadist violence, and U.S. forces struck jihadist camps in northwestern Nigeria on Christmas Day. Rights organizations have cautioned against overstating the religious dimension of Nigeria's broader security crisis, which also involves criminal and ethnic conflicts.

stories.headline: Shell Knew Nigeria Pipeline Was Causing Widespread Pollution for Years, Internal Documents Show
stories.summary:
Internal Shell documents obtained by the BBC show that the company continued operating a major oil pipeline in Nigeria's Niger Delta for years after a senior executive warned in 2008 of serious pollution risks stemming from large-scale theft, illegal refining, and infrastructure failures along the line. The documents, including emails and presentations, were disclosed as part of ongoing UK legal proceedings brought by communities near the Nembe Creek Trunk Line seeking $1 billion in damages.

The 60-mile pipeline, capable of carrying up to 150,000 barrels per day and sold by Shell last year, was repeatedly hit by spills between 2011 and 2013. Residents of Bille, a community of 45 islands near the pipeline, described once-thriving fishing grounds turning toxic, with fish populations collapsing or appearing deformed. Fisherman Balafama Augustus Bruce, a plaintiff in the lawsuit, told the BBC he has been reduced to poverty by the destruction of the fishery he depended on.

Shell argues in court filings that the majority of pollution resulted from third-party "large-scale oil theft, sabotage," and dozens of illegal refineries, and that its Nigerian subsidiary invested heavily in spill prevention and response. The case represents one of the largest environmental liability claims ever brought against an international oil major and could set significant legal precedents for corporate accountability for environmental harm in developing nations.

The United Nations has documented at least 13 million barrels of crude oil spilled in the Niger Delta since Shell began operating there in 1958 — one of the world's most severe cases of oil-related environmental damage. The BBC's investigation, based on the newly disclosed internal records, adds documentary evidence to longstanding community and activist claims that Shell was aware of the risks and continued operations regardless.

stories.headline: U.S. Announces New Tariffs on Nearly All Trading Partners Over Forced Labour Concerns
stories.summary:
The Trump administration has announced new tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on roughly 60 trading partners — including the United Kingdom, European Union, Canada, India, Japan and China — that together account for nearly all U.S. imports. The U.S. Trade Representative's office said the duties stem from those countries' failure to prohibit or effectively enforce bans on importing goods made with forced labour. The tariffs have not yet taken effect and must go through a formal implementation process.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer framed the action as correcting an uneven playing field for American workers. The move marks the second major round of tariffs announced by the Trump administration since the Supreme Court struck down many of its earlier duties in February, this time using forced labour as the legal rationale rather than national security or trade balance.

Affected governments pushed back sharply. The UK said it is actively tackling forced labour in its supply chains and is engaged in ongoing trade negotiations with Washington. China denied that any forced labour exists within its borders, calling the tariffs 'political manipulation.' The EU called the duties unjustified and said it remains committed to the trade deal reached with the Trump administration last year. An India analyst described the move as a pressure tactic ahead of broader negotiations.

The announcement carries significant economic implications, touching virtually every major U.S. trading relationship. China and India face the higher 12.5 percent rate, while Canada, the EU, the UK and others face 10 percent. The administration's move also raises questions about how courts will treat this new justification for tariffs given the earlier Supreme Court ruling.

stories.headline: Fire Kills at Least 21 in Delhi Building Housing Foreign Medical Patients
stories.summary:
A fire tore through a multi-storey building in the Malviya Nagar area of south Delhi early Wednesday, killing at least 21 people and injuring dozens more. The building operated as a bed-and-breakfast catering to patients and relatives of those receiving treatment at a nearby private hospital, and many victims were foreign nationals, including people from Bangladesh and other South Asian countries as well as African and Central Asian nations who had traveled to India for medical care.

More than 40 people were rescued and taken to hospital. Emergency workers found numerous victims unconscious inside hotel rooms and washrooms. Some occupants jumped from upper floors to escape the flames; a local shopkeeper spread quilts on the ground below to cushion those attempting to jump. The fire was brought under control relatively quickly, but the cause remains unknown.

Delhi Minister Ashish Sood said authorities are investigating whether the building had the necessary legal permissions to operate as a bed-and-breakfast. Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressed condolences and announced compensation of 200,000 rupees for families of the dead and 50,000 rupees for the injured. Officials said those found responsible for any regulatory violations would face criminal action.

The blaze is described as one of the deadliest fires in recent years in the Indian capital. Fires are common in India, where building safety regulations are frequently flouted, and the death toll among vulnerable foreign nationals traveling for medical treatment adds an international dimension to the tragedy.

stories.headline: EU Unveils Sweeping Tech Sovereignty Plan Targeting Chips, AI and Cloud Independence
stories.summary:
The European Union announced a comprehensive technology sovereignty initiative on Wednesday aimed at expanding domestic supply chains in semiconductors, artificial intelligence and cloud computing. The plan is designed to reduce European dependence on the United States and Asia for critical digital infrastructure, reflecting growing concern in Brussels that reliance on foreign technology platforms poses strategic risks.

The initiative comes at a moment of heightened transatlantic tension, with new U.S. tariffs announced the same day covering nearly all EU imports and ongoing disputes over digital regulation between Washington and Brussels. The EU has been pressing to build indigenous capacity in advanced chips and AI since supply chain disruptions during the pandemic exposed vulnerabilities in European industry.

Few details of the specific funding mechanisms or timelines were immediately available, but the plan is described as sweeping in scope, covering the full technology stack from hardware to software. It follows previous EU efforts such as the European Chips Act and the AI Act, and signals that the bloc intends to accelerate its push for strategic autonomy in technology even as it navigates trade frictions with its major partners.

The announcement positions the EU as a third pole in global technology competition alongside the United States and China at a time when AI investment and semiconductor supply chains are central to economic and national security calculations worldwide.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Strikes St. Petersburg Oil Terminal; Drone Hits Bus in Russia-Controlled Territory, Killing Seven
stories.summary:
Ukraine launched a sweeping overnight drone offensive striking Russian territory, including a hit on an oil terminal in St. Petersburg as the city hosts the annual International Economic Forum. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the strike, calling it part of Ukraine's "long-range sanctions" campaign, while Russian aviation authorities temporarily restricted flights at Pulkovo airport. Russia says it shot down 350 Ukrainian drones overnight.

Separately, seven civilians were killed and 11 injured when a drone struck a passenger bus traveling between Moscow and Simferopol through Russia-controlled Donetsk. Denis Pushilin, the Kremlin-installed regional leader, blamed Ukraine for the attack; Ukrainian officials pushed back, characterizing Russian claims as propaganda designed to equate Ukrainian strikes with Russia's systematic attacks on civilian infrastructure.

The exchanges come one day after a massive Russian assault killed at least 23 people across Ukraine, including women and children. An 86-year-old woman was also killed in a separate overnight drone attack on Ukraine's Kherson region. The intensifying tit-for-tat strikes underscore the continued escalation of the war with no ceasefire in sight.

Russian President Vladimir Putin is expected to address International Economic Forum delegates in St. Petersburg on Friday, making the timing of the Ukrainian strike on the city particularly pointed. The forum is designed to project economic normalcy and attract international business to Russia despite ongoing Western sanctions.

stories.headline: Suspect Killed After Opening Fire Outside White House; Identified as Maryland Man With Prior Secret Service Encounters
stories.summary:
A man opened fire outside the White House on Saturday afternoon and was shot by U.S. Secret Service agents. The suspect, identified as Nasire Best, 21, of Maryland, died en route to George Washington University Medical Center. The incident drew coverage from 18 news outlets, reflecting its significance as a direct security threat to the executive mansion.

Best had multiple prior encounters with the Secret Service. He was detained on June 26, 2025, after flagging down agents and making threats, and again on July 10, 2025, for entering a restricted area. Sources described him as having a history of mental health issues.

The incident raises fresh questions about perimeter security at the White House and the handling of individuals who have previously made threats against or near the complex. No other injuries were reported.

stories.headline: Update: Kuwait Airport Damaged by Iranian Drones as U.S.-Iran Conflict Widens; Israel Threatens Beirut Strikes Again
stories.summary:
Kuwait's international airport sustained significant damage from Iranian drone strikes, with traffic suspended, marking a major escalation in the widening U.S.-Iran conflict that has already drawn Gulf states into its orbit. Kuwait has condemned what it called "repeated" Iranian attacks on its territory. The strikes follow previous Iranian missile attacks on U.S. troops stationed in Kuwait and come as nuclear negotiations remain stalled over U.S. demands related to the Strait of Hormuz and the removal of highly enriched uranium.

On the Israeli-Hezbollah front, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Beirut suburbs would be targeted in response to attacks on Israeli civilians, prompting thousands to flee Hezbollah's stronghold of Dahieh. Israel has not yet struck Beirut following a U.S.-brokered deal announcement, but the ceasefire with Hezbollah appears fragile. Israel also called its capture of Beaufort Castle a "decisive shift" in its Lebanon campaign, drawing criticism from European governments.

BBC analysis indicates Iran's strikes on U.S. military positions have been more extensive than publicly acknowledged, with satellite imagery showing damage to at least 20 U.S. military sites since the start of the conflict. Analysts say neither side appears to want all-out war, but the cycle of strikes and stalled negotiations continues to escalate regional risk.

The conflict is placing acute strain on global shipping, with some 20,000 seafarers reported trapped in the war zone. The White House is under pressure from Gulf allies and domestic polling to broker a deal, but Iran is demanding concessions the U.S. has so far resisted.

stories.headline: FBI Launches Nationwide Summer Crime Initiative After 35 Charged in West Virginia Drug and Firearms Operation
stories.summary:
The FBI announced Tuesday that 35 people had been charged with narcotics and firearms offenses stemming from Operation Turf War, a yearlong federal investigation in West Virginia conducted by FBI Pittsburgh and FBI Baltimore alongside the Eastern Panhandle Drug and Violent Crimes Task Force. The operation resulted in the seizure of illegal firearms, drugs, and proceeds tied to violent criminal activity. FBI Director Kash Patel called it "a massively successful operation" demonstrating what law enforcement partnerships "are supposed to look like."

Alongside the West Virginia arrests, the FBI launched Operation Summer Heat 2.0, a nationwide violent crime initiative running through September 20. The effort is modeled on last year's Operation Summer Heat, which the bureau said resulted in more than 8,600 arrests, nearly 7,750 search operations, the seizure of 2,280 firearms, and more than 44,560 kilograms of cocaine. This year's initiative is described as larger in scope, with expanded federal-state-local coordination.

The announcement reflects the Trump administration's continued emphasis on aggressive federal law enforcement engagement at the local level, a priority that has been both praised by Republican allies as a necessary crackdown on crime and scrutinized by civil liberties advocates concerned about the expansion of federal policing roles.
